work: Designing Programmes, 1964
take: The Capital grid of 1962: a page 58 units wide with 2-unit gutters, which carries one to six columns of whole units.

work: With Dashboards, Formatting and Layout Definitely Matter, 2008
take: Counts the rigid symmetrical grid among the layout mistakes of dashboard design.

work: Grid Systems in Graphic Design, 1981
take: The standard manual of grid construction. It calls the grid an aid, not a guarantee.

work: The Typographic Grid, 2000
take: About two dozen of the author’s own works with the grids behind them, and no single recipe.

work: Unigrid, 1977
take: One sheet system for the brochures of more than 400 parks. The first brochure to use it appeared in 1978.

work: Sparkline theory and practice, from Beautiful Evidence, 2006
take: Word-sized graphics that set a value beside its history, with a grey band for the normal range in the medical examples.

work: Bullet Graph Design Specification, 2006, revised 2013
take: The formal definition: a featured measure, a comparator and optional qualitative ranges.

work: Graphic Methods for Presenting Facts, 1914
take: An early American manual of charts for business, free on the Internet Archive and still a good source of component-bar forms.

work: Charting Statistics, 1952
take: Her range bar, with an interquartile box, predates the box plot. A compact way to show spread within a row.

work: The High Performance HMI Handbook, 2008
take: Grey screens, analog indicators with a normal range, and colour only for abnormal states.

work: ANSI/ISA-101.01-2015, human-machine interfaces for process automation systems
take: Sets out a life cycle for process displays around each site’s written HMI philosophy and style guide. It does not itself prescribe grey screens; that comes from high-performance HMI practice.

work: Information Rich Design, Halden
take: Large-screen process overviews built from aligned mini-trends and Gestalt grouping.

work: Why I stopped using bullet graphs, Nightingale, 2022
take: Eleven objections. Problems do not stand out, and lower-is-better and ideal-range measures need variants. His alternative marks only what crosses an action threshold.

work: The Amazon Weekly Business Review, Commoncog, 2024
take: Amazon’s weekly review of 400 to 500 metrics, most drawn as one chart: the trailing six weeks beside the trailing twelve months.

work: Graphical summary of patient status, The Lancet, 1994
take: Small aligned histories with normal ranges on one page. A clinical ancestor of the sparkline.

work: Understanding Variation, 1993
take: Process behaviour charts separate routine weekly variation from a real change. A stronger comparator than last period once history exists.

work: The Commercial and Political Atlas, 1786
take: Import and export lines with the area between them tinted as the balance. An early case of an accounting identity drawn as a shape.

work: Ecological interface design: theoretical foundations, IEEE SMC 1992
take: Make the constraints of the work domain directly visible. The theory behind drawing an identity as geometry.

work: Display and Interface Design: Subtle Science, Exact Art, 2011
take: Configural displays and emergent features. When variables are drawn so their relationship forms a shape, a fault changes the shape.

work: Cartographic Relief Presentation, 1965; Envisioning Information, chapter 5
take: Strong colour in small areas on a muted ground, and large areas kept quiet. The rule behind one accent on tonal surfaces.

work: The Look of Maps, 1952
take: Visual hierarchy and figure and ground in cartography. Maps solved layered surfaces long before interfaces did.

work: Shaded relief practice and research
take: How Swiss-style relief generalises terrain and adjusts light locally. Shading as a selective, designed act.

work: Common region: a new principle of perceptual grouping, Cognitive Psychology, 1992
take: Elements inside a shared boundary group strongly and hierarchically. The basis for nested surfaces, and the reason every panel boundary is a claim.

work: Interaction of Color, 1963
take: A colour is read relative to its surround.

work: Graphical perception, JASA 1984; crowdsourced replication, CHI 2010
take: Position on a common scale is read most accurately; shade and area least.

work: Modeling color difference for visualization design, 2018; In color perception, size matters, 2012
take: Small marks need larger colour differences to be told apart. Thin lines and 3 px bars cannot rely on subtle tints.

work: Transparent layered user interfaces, CHI 1995
take: Measured how translucency trades focus against awareness. The evidence for and against see-through panels.

work: Transparency and blur as selective cues, 1991; Information Landscapes, 1994
take: The MIT Visible Language Workshop treated translucency, blur and depth as information design. An origin of the soft layered look.

work: Material 3 colour roles; Radix 12-step scales
take: Two working role systems. Material names five container tones by emphasis. Radix gives each of twelve steps a job.

work: Carbon Design System, colour and layering
take: Surface roles as named tokens. In the light themes, layers alternate between white and a pale grey.

work: WCAG 2.2, non-text contrast
take: The parts of a control or a graphic that a reader must see need a contrast of at least three to one against what is next to them.

work: Solid, Outlined, Hatched, 2019, and the IBCS standard
take: A notation for reports: solid for actual, outlined for plan, hatched for forecast, grey for the prior period.

work: Semiology of Graphics, 1967
take: Names the visual variables a mark can vary by, texture among them. The link is a summary.

work: Train graph, La Méthode graphique, 1878
take: Distance against time, with speed as slope. A whole timetable on one pair of axes.

work: The reorderable matrix; Bertifier, IEEE VIS 2014
take: Encode each cell, then reorder rows and columns until structure appears.

work: The visual design and control of Trellis display, JCGS 1996
take: Panels conditioned on a variable, laid out in rows and columns with shared scales.

work: Graphical perception of multiple time series, IEEE TVCG 2010
take: Separate small charts were generally more efficient for comparisons across many series, and one shared chart for comparisons close together.

work: Polaris, IEEE TVCG 2002
take: A table algebra that nests small charts by dimension. The research behind Tableau.

work: Ensemble meteograms, Forecast User Guide 8.1.4
take: Several weather parameters stacked on one time axis, each drawn as box-and-whisker steps.

work: WSSI: weekly sales, stock and intake
take: The planner’s native grid. Weeks across; sales, stock and intake down; open-to-buy as its result.

work: Visual momentum, International Journal of Man-Machine Studies, 1984
take: How to keep a reader oriented across many displays: an overview, landmarks, overlap and fixed positions.

work: Guidelines for using multiple views in information visualization, AVI 2000
take: Eight rules, including parsimony: add a view only when it earns its cost.

work: Visual comparison for information visualization, 2011
take: Every comparison is built from juxtaposition, superposition or an explicit encoding of the difference.

work: Schedule for all sports disciplines, Munich 1972
take: Dates, events and pictograms cross-indexed on one sheet, printed on both sides in seven colours.

work: Visualization Analysis and Design, 2014
take: A framework of what, why and how, with rules of thumb. Eyes beat memory: compare side by side, not from recollection.

work: Brushing scatterplots, Technometrics, 1987
take: Named brushing: a selection made in one view marks the same items in every other view. The link is a summary.

work: Cross-view brushing
take: A design pattern for highlighting selected items across several representations.

work: Untidy data: the unreasonable effectiveness of tables, IEEE TVCG 2022
take: Data workers want to see and touch the table throughout analysis. Tables are a visualization idiom in their own right.

work: Rudiments of numeracy, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society A, 1977
take: The classic paper on numeric tables: round hard, order rows by size, and put figures to be compared in columns.

work: Ten guidelines for better tables, Journal of Benefit-Cost Analysis, 2020
take: A modern checklist: right-align numbers, show units sparingly, lighten the rules.

work: Tschichold’s table rules, quoted by Rutter, 2017
take: Set tables as text to be read, keep furniture to a minimum, avoid vertical rules.

work: The Table Lens, CHI 1994
take: A table whose cells become small bars, with rows that open to text on focus. Bertin’s in-cell bars, brought to the screen.

work: LineUp, IEEE InfoVis 2013
take: Ranks items on several weighted attributes with stacked bars inside a table.

work: Catalog Design Progress, 1950
take: Product information designed as function, flow and form. The classic on structuring commercial data for fast lookup.

work: Dutch telephone directory, 1977
take: Condensed Univers, lower case only, numbers placed before names so no leader dots were needed.

work: A schema for the study of graphic language, 1979
take: Classifies graphic language by configuration, including list, matrix and branching. Useful vocabulary for deciding what a view is.

work: Bell Centennial, 1975–78
take: Drawn for telephone directories printed fast on poor paper.

work: Retina, 1999
take: Drawn for Wall Street Journal stock listings at very small sizes, now in the MoMA collection. Type as an instrument for dense figures.

work: Univers, 1957
take: Twenty-one variants named by a two-digit code for weight and width, planned as one family from the start.

work: Roboto Flex and the grade axis
take: Grade changes apparent weight without changing width. Useful in dark mode, where light text looks heavier.

work: Instrument Sans
take: An open variable family with a 75 to 100 width axis and tabular figures. The sans used on this page.

work: Typographie, 1967
take: A manual on rhythm, proportion and the space inside and around letters, from the Basel school.

work: Detail in Typography, 1987
take: Letters, letterspacing, words, wordspacing, lines and linespacing in sixty-four pages.

work: The Inflation Report projections: understanding the fan chart, Bank of England, 1998
take: The fan chart, first published in February 1996, shows a forecast as nested probability bands in place of a line with bounds.

work: When (ish) is My Bus?, CHI 2016
take: Introduced quantile dotplots: a distribution as about twenty countable dots. Readers estimated probabilities more consistently than from density curves.

work: Uncertainty displays using quantile dotplots or CDFs improve transit decision-making, CHI 2018
take: Decision quality, measured. Dotplots and cumulative curves beat intervals and point estimates.

work: Hypothetical outcome plots, PLOS ONE 2015
take: Animated draws from a distribution outperformed error bars and violins for judging which of two quantities is larger.

work: Error bars considered harmful, IEEE TVCG 2014
take: Bars with whiskers make values inside the bar look likelier than values outside it.

work: Uncertainty forecasts improve weather-related decisions, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 2012
take: Showing uncertainty improved decisions and softened the effect of a forecast that missed.

work: Uncertainty visualization, Wiley StatsRef, 2021
take: The best single review: the techniques, the psychology behind each, and frequency framing.

work: The Flaw of Averages, 2009
take: Plans built on average demand are wrong on average. An argument for planning against a distribution once one exists.

work: Dynamic queries for visual information seeking, IEEE Software, 1994
take: Results update within a tenth of a second as sliders move, so a query becomes something to steer.

work: Interactive dynamics for visual analysis, Communications of the ACM, 2012
take: Twelve tasks in three groups: specifying data and views, manipulating views, and recording and sharing the analysis.

work: Up and Down the Ladder of Abstraction, 2011
take: An interactive essay that moves between one concrete case and the whole range of a parameter.

work: Explorable Explanations, 2011
take: Reactive documents: a number in a sentence can be dragged, and the text recomputes.

work: Is It Better to Rent or Buy?, The New York Times, 2014
take: Each slider sits on a small chart of the outcome across the whole range of that input.

work: Visual parameter space analysis, IEEE TVCG 2014
take: A framework for exploring model inputs and outputs: a data flow, four navigation strategies and six tasks.

work: Decision analysis: practice and promise, Management Science, 1988
take: Usually cited for the tornado diagram: one-way sensitivities sorted by swing, each input moved between assessed low and high values. A form for ranking assumptions by their effect on a result.

work: Effective forecasting and judgmental adjustments, International Journal of Forecasting, 2009
take: Small overrides tended to hurt accuracy, large reasoned ones helped, and adjustments leaned optimistic.

work: Forecast value added: a reality check, Foresight, 2013
take: Compare each step of the process with a naive forecast. The stairstep report shows where review adds or removes value.

work: Plain Words, 1948
take: Written at the request of the British Treasury to help officials replace jargon with a short, clear style. The link describes its editions.

work: The rhetoric of neutrality, Design Issues, 1985
take: Even a railway timetable persuades. A calm analytical style is a rhetorical choice and should be owned as one.

g: Further reading · forecasting and retail practice
work: Retail forecasting: research and practice, International Journal of Forecasting, 2022
take: The standard review of retail forecasting, from strategic decisions down to store and item.

g: Further reading · forecasting and retail practice
work: Making supply meet demand in an uncertain world, Harvard Business Review, 1994
take: Sport Obermeyer, a skiwear maker, planned its buying around how uncertain each style’s demand was.

g: Further reading · forecasting and retail practice
work: Demand Forecasting for Executives and Professionals, 2023
take: A current, readable text with an online edition.

g: Further reading · forecasting and retail practice
work: Demand Forecasting Best Practices, 2023
take: Practical guidance on metrics: track bias and absolute error together and avoid MAPE.

g: Further reading · forecasting and retail practice
work: On the categorization of demand patterns, Journal of the Operational Research Society, 2005
take: Classes items as smooth, erratic, intermittent or lumpy from two statistics, with cut-offs at 1.32 and 0.49.

g: Further reading · forecasting and retail practice
work: Optimal forecast reconciliation through trace minimization, JASA, 2019
take: Forecasts at item, category and total level can be made to add up.

g: Further reading · forecasting and retail practice
work: The M5 accuracy competition, International Journal of Forecasting, 2022
take: 42,840 hierarchical Walmart series with many zeros. Evidence on what works for intermittent retail demand.

g: Further reading · forecasting and retail practice
work: Analytics for an online retailer, Manufacturing and Service Operations Management, 2016
take: Demand forecasting and price optimisation at Rue La La, an online fashion retailer, with a measured revenue effect.

g: Further reading · forecasting and retail practice
work: Clearance pricing optimization for a fast-fashion retailer, Operations Research, 2012
take: Zara’s markdown process, tested in a field experiment.

g: Further reading · forecasting and retail practice
work: The newsvendor critical ratio
take: For a single buy before a season, the best service level is the underage cost over the sum of underage and overage cost. A principled source for a stock target.

g: Further reading · forecasting and retail practice
work: Prioritized ordering
take: Rank every possible purchase unit by expected economic return and buy down the list until the budget is spent. An alternative to item-by-item alerts.

g: Further reading · forecasting and retail practice
work: Industrial Dynamics, 1961; Business Dynamics, 2000
take: Stock-and-flow notation. Inventory is a stock; sales and receipts are flows.

work: What do we talk about when we talk about dashboards?, IEEE TVCG 2019
take: A design space and typology of dashboards, built from a survey of the kinds in use.

who: Bach, Freeman, Abdul-Rahman, Turkay, Khan, Fan, Chen
work: Dashboard design patterns, IEEE TVCG 2023
take: Forty-one patterns for content and composition, with the trade-offs between screen space, paging and abstraction.

work: The science of visual data communication: what works, PSPI 2021
take: The most complete review of what is known to work, written for practitioners.

work: Graphical overlays, IEEE TVCG 2012
take: Five kinds of layered aid: reference structures, highlights, redundant encodings, summary statistics and annotations.

work: Striking a balance, IEEE TVCG 2023
take: Readers preferred charts with text over charts alone. Put words at the mark.

work: Sizing the horizon, CHI 2009
take: Horizon graphs keep a time series readable at small heights, with measured limits on how small.

work: UI Density, 2024
take: Density is the value delivered per unit of space and time, with visual, information and temporal components.

who: Bateman and colleagues; Inbar, Tractinsky, Meyer
work: Useful junk?, CHI 2010; Minimalism in information visualization, 2007
take: Counter-evidence to strict minimalism. Embellished charts were recalled better, and people did not prefer the most reduced bar chart.

work: Functional Aesthetics for Data Visualization, 2022
take: Perception, semantics and intent treated together.
